name: Carla Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work weekdays for a national agency's branch in a new commuter town, full of estates built for people who work in the city. I do six or seven calls from seven till two, then on Saturdays I run my own little side line, doing companion visits and shopping for two private clients. First call is Mrs Novak, a Polish widow who likes her tea strong and her radio loud. I plan my whole week with an AI assistant on my phone, routes and shopping lists and all.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the Saturday work best, because it's mine and I set the price. The weekday work wears me out because the branch rota is a mess and I'm still slow with some of the clinical stuff, like catheter care. Mark, my husband, drives buses, and between us we cover the rent on a little terrace, but we've got about three weeks' money in the bank. We married young, at twenty-two, and we're saving for a family, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, AI's still useful for the small stuff. I'd post a tip on the carers' group about how I plan my routes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm a bit disappointed, because I was hoping AI would help me grow the Saturday work. But my job's safe, and there's more old people moving to the estates every year. It's the money that's tight, not the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekday job and grow the Saturday clients to four, using AI to write the adverts and do the invoices. I'd do the catheter training the branch keeps offering, to get better. And I'd put Saturday money aside for when we start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit restless, but fine. Even if AI is mostly hype, AI still writes my Saturday adverts while I'm on the bus between clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Saturday clients. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Novak's son asked if I'd do weekends privately, because the agency doesn't cover them. Then his friend's dad asked. I registered as self-employed, did it all properly. It brings in about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money worry that sits with you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's bus route. The council keeps talking about cutting routes, and if he lost his shifts we'd be in trouble fast. That, and we want a baby before thirty, but not until we've got some savings.

I'd post a **route-planning tip** on the carers' group.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, hoping AI would grow my Saturday work.
My job's **safe**, with more old people moving to the estates.
do: Grow the **Saturday clients** to four, using AI for adverts and invoices.
Do the **catheter training** the branch keeps offering.
Save the **Saturday money** for starting a family.

She uses AI **daily** for routes, adverts and invoices.

steps.text: Grow the Saturday companion business from two clients to four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance for carers who are willing to learn. I'd tell people at the branch to stop moaning and start using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. The thinking bits, the booking, invoicing, rotas, AI does all of that, which means I can run more Saturday clients without drowning in paperwork. My hands-on work is safe for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the Saturday work into a proper little business, maybe five or six clients, using AI for bookings and invoices. I'd keep the weekday job for steady money. I'd learn every AI tool going, including the branch's new notes app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about Mark. AI doing my bookings and invoices means a carer like me can run a small business from my phone on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your work would AI take, and what would that free up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bookings, invoices, rotas, and the care notes. That frees up maybe five hours a week, which I'd spend on more clients. That's real money for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Mark, driving buses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the worry. Robots spread slowly into hands-on work here, so buses might be okay for a bit, but the planning and ticketing go to AI. I'd tell him to look at driving for my business one day, if it grows.

I'd tell people at the branch to **start using** the tools.

My **hands-on work** is safe for years.

fieldNote: Carla sees Steady Disruption as **fuel** for her own business.
She values AI freeing **five hours** a week for paid client time.
She'd consider bringing **Mark** into the business one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get moving, now. I'd say it's no use waiting for the government, families and businesses have to sort themselves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's frightening, because both me and Mark would be hit. AI by 2028 does all the thinking work, which I like, but robots by 2031 would do the care and maybe drive the buses. I'd be thirty-one with a tiny business that robots can do cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business fast in those three years, then try to become the person who places and supervises robots for families. I'd use AI for everything, from marketing to accounts. And we'd put off the baby, which would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. My husband Mark and I wanted a baby before thirty. Robots doing care by 2031 would mean choosing between a family and keeping a roof over our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots by 2031. What happens to your business in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to grow it fast, maybe hire one or two carers, so I'm the owner, not the hands. Then in 2031, I'd switch to running robots for families who want someone they trust in charge. But it's a big gamble with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put them off, for sure. Mark would say wait, and he'd be right. That would be the worst part, honestly.

fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens **both incomes** in Carla's household.
She'd try to become the **owner**, not the hands, before robots arrive.
Delaying a **baby** is the cost that hurts her most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so use it. I'd tell other carers to learn the tools and maybe start something of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one I think I could handle. I'd grow the business steadily, maybe have a baby in the middle, and be ready for robots in 2034. Mark's buses would be the worry still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business to eight or ten clients over a few years, hire a couple of carers, and use AI for everything behind the scenes. I'd save for a family. And I'd keep an eye out for robot suppliers to partner with by 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a good way. With five years, I could own a small care business that runs the robots instead of being one of the carers the robots replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years before thinking AI, eight before robots. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes, for the steady money. Then I'd go full time on the business. It's risky, but it's the only way I'd ever get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep the weekday job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark would keep driving as long as he could. Maybe he'd join the business doing transport for clients. We'd see.

S3.quote: With five years, I could own a small care business that runs the robots instead of being one of the carers the robots replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who works hard can come out on top. I'd encourage people to start small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. I'd have a family, a business, and time to learn the robot side properly. Mark could retrain if his buses went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business over five years, have a baby, and save for a house. I'd learn robot supervision when it came. I'd keep using AI for everything behind the scenes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Ten years is enough for me, a carer who left school at sixteen, to run a business with my own staff and robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What does your business look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A team of carers and maybe some robots, run from a little office or my kitchen table. Families paying for someone they trust to be in charge. That's the dream, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want the government to do, given how you feel about handouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help for small businesses and apprenticeships, yes. Not handouts. Make it easy to start something and hire people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to build the business, and both Mark and I would be hit before we'd had a baby. What would help is easy loans or grants for small care businesses, and training for people like Mark. I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it, and that takes time and a little bit of money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what families can afford. Robots will be cheaper than us, so the families who can't pay for people now might finally get some help. That's not all bad.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it, and that takes time and a little bit of money.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** agency carer in a commuter town who runs her own Saturday care business.
She married **Mark**, a bus driver, at twenty-two, and they're saving to start a family.
She uses AI **every day** for routes, adverts and invoices.
She's uneasy in slow pictures and **alarmed** under fast AGI, when both incomes are at risk.
Her plan is to **own** the business that runs the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to build the business before both she and Mark are hit.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **loans or grants** for small care businesses.
